notes:
I've drafted notes for most of James 4, but the research hit its search and page limits early. I fully read only one page (Enduring Word / Guzik). Everything else comes from search-result excerpts, so these notes cover less than you asked for:

- **Not covered at all:** Catholic and Orthodox readings, Bible Odyssey, and prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching.
- **Covered thinly:** vv. 11–12 and 17 rest on one source each, and v. 16 only on short mentions.
- **Section 2 (Protestant traditions):** I found no real differences that line up by denomination. The only big split is over verse 5, and it runs between individual commentators.

---

**v. 1:** Guzik says James uses "wars and fights" because quarrels among Christians are often bitter and severe. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-4/ He traces the fighting to selfish desires in the flesh. People who quarrel often claim the Spirit is behind them, but James says it comes from their own desires. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-4/

**v. 2:** Guzik (on the full page) links "kill" to Jesus treating anger as murder of the heart (Matthew 5:21–22). He sees the "you do not have" as showing how unsatisfying a life of selfish desire is. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-4/ On "you do not ask," he says believers can live as spiritual paupers simply because they don't pray, or don't ask when they do. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-4/

**v. 3:** Guzik says James moves from the problem of no prayer to the problem of selfish prayer. Prayer isn't for talking God into doing our will but for lining our will up with his. He also notes that "squander" is the same verb used of the Prodigal Son's wasteful spending. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-4/

**v. 4:**
- Guzik says "adulteresses" is Old Testament language for idolatry, picturing God as husband and his people as wife (Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Hosea). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-4/
- He notes that better manuscripts have only the feminine "adulteresses." He thinks "adulterers" was added by a scribe who took the word literally. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-4/
- Even wanting to be the world's friend makes a person God's enemy. Guzik also says the verse warns against romanticising the early church. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-4/

**v. 5: the hardest verse, and the main real disagreement.**
- **Text:** NET notes that the older manuscripts have the verb meaning "caused to dwell." That makes "spirit" the thing God placed in us. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=jam&chapter=4&verse=5
- **View A: God or the Holy Spirit jealously longs for us.**
  - Guzik: the Spirit within us has a jealous yearning for our friendship with God and will convict compromise. He says either wording gives much the same sense. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-4/
  - Ellicott: the Spirit wants us wholly for himself and won't accept divided loyalty. He reads the Greek word for "envy" the way other writers used "jealousy," as a picture of pure love. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/james/4-5.htm
  - Calvin (studylight): some take "spirit" to mean the human soul, but those who see God's Spirit "think better." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/james/4-5.html
  - Got Questions also prefers the Holy Spirit. It grants that the human-spirit view fits the warning against worldliness, but says it fits "dwells in us" less well. https://www.gotquestions.org/Spirit-yearns-jealously.html
- **View B: the human spirit, which leans toward envy.**
  - Barnes: the Holy Spirit reading is "forced and unnatural." He takes the verse to mean we are naturally prone to envy. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/esv/james/4-5.html
  - NET's translators also prefer this. They say the word for "envy" is generally negative in the Bible and the surrounding verses favour the negative reading. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=jam&chapter=4&verse=5
  - Precept Austin cites a source (the MSB) holding that "spirit" is the human spirit and the phrase means "lusts to envy." https://www.preceptaustin.org/james_45_commentary
- **Middle view:** God is the one who yearns, and the human spirit is what he yearns for. Either way, God wants us to belong to him wholeheartedly. https://www.preceptaustin.org/james_45_commentary
- **"The Scripture says":** Guzik notes the words appear in no single Old Testament verse. James is probably summing up several passages about God's jealousy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-4/

**v. 6:** Guzik says the Spirit who convicts us also gives grace to serve God. "Opposes" means God lines up for battle against the proud. Humility doesn't earn grace; it puts us in a position to receive it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-4/

**v. 7:**
- **Submit:** Guzik says it means surrendering to God as a conquering King. He passes on Spurgeon's reasons to submit: God created us, his rule is good for us, and resisting him is futile. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-4/
- **Resist the devil:** Guzik points out that James doesn't tell a third party to cast demons out of believers. Each Christian is to stand against Satan personally, as a defeated foe. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-4/

**v. 8:** Guzik says drawing near is both an invitation and a promise, made possible by Christ's blood. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-4/ He passes on Barclay: the word "sinner" here means someone whose sin is open and well known. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-4/

**v. 9:** Through Moffatt, Guzik says James is using the Hebrew prophets' language for the anguish of repentance. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-4/

**v. 10:** Guzik says we come before God as sinners, not self-righteous (Luke 18). Grace, God's unearned favour, always lifts people up. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-4/

**vv. 11–12:** Guzik says getting right with God has to show in how we speak about others. To judge a brother is to put yourself in the law's place. There is one Lawgiver, so humility leaves no room for judging. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-4/

**v. 13:**
- Piper (Desiring God) says James may be addressing merchants, but the warning is broad enough to include almost anyone. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/if-the-lord-wills
- Sam Storms says James isn't condemning planning, business or honest profit. He condemns planning that doesn't humbly admit God controls the future. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/if-the-lord-wills-james-413-17

**v. 14:** Guzik says James is stressing how fragile life is. He doesn't forbid planning, only planning that ignores God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-4/

**v. 15:**
- Piper: what we achieve, not just how long we live, is in God's hands. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/if-the-lord-wills
- Barnes: we don't need to say the words constantly, which could become empty show. We should shape every plan around God's will. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/james/4-15.htm
- A homiletical commentary on studylight warns against writing "D.V." ("God willing") everywhere as a formality. Coffman, by contrast, urges Christians to actually say "If the Lord will," sincerely. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/james/4-13.html, https://www.studylight.org/commentary/james/4-15.html
- One commentator on biblehub (name not shown in the excerpt) says this is far from fatalism. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/james/4-15.htm

**v. 16:** Storms: thinking we are masters of our own fate is the arrogance James calls "evil." https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/if-the-lord-wills-james-413-17

**v. 17:** Matthew Henry ties this to v. 15. Readers might say everyone knows we depend on God, but if you know it and act otherwise, the sin is greater. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jam/Jam_004.cfm
